headline: Bots at the Till, Chips on Hold, Dams on Thin Ice
teaser: Would you let an AI pay for your shopping? Can export rules control computing power that travels through cables? And should Nepal build giant dams on melting mountains?

articles.title: Agents at the Checkout: Why Shoppers Still Won't Let AI Pay
articles.dek: AI now helps millions of people find gifts, yet almost nobody lets it pay. Is that caution sensible, or just the early nervousness every new technology faces?
paras: This year's Black Friday was supposed to be the moment artificial intelligence took over holiday shopping. According to early figures from Adobe, traffic from AI services to American retail websites more than doubled on Thanksgiving compared with last year, while shoppers spent a record $7.1 billion online that day, up 10.4 percent. Yet when it comes to actually completing a purchase, the machines are still sitting on the bench. Research by the consultancy Bain & Company found that AI agents accounted for just 0.4 percent of global e-commerce transactions and only 0.2 percent of their value.

To understand that gap, it helps to separate two kinds of tools. An AI assistant answers questions: it suggests gift ideas, summarises reviews and compares prices. An AI agent goes further and acts on the user's behalf, searching shops, filling a basket and paying. Technology companies are betting heavily on the second kind. Meta's shopping agent, Muse, reportedly reached 10 million users in the United States and Canada about six weeks after its September launch, and this week it arrived in Britain. The consultancy McKinsey estimates that this so-called agentic commerce could generate $1 trillion of economic activity in the US by 2030.

Consumers, however, are drawing a clear line between asking and delegating. A Morning Consult poll for Visa found that 54 percent of adults have used AI for at least one shopping task, up from 47 percent a year earlier, but only 23 percent trust generative AI to make payments for them. An American Express survey points to the same pattern: 52 percent of US consumers are happy for an agent to buy cheap, routine items such as groceries, but just 15 percent feel the same about electronics or appliances. In other words, people are willing to hand over decisions only when a mistake would cost them little.

Their caution is not irrational. When Visa tested 22 AI models on 15 shopping tasks earlier this month, they failed 42.8 percent of the runs, and in more than half of those failed runs the agent still bought something. Maia Bittner, a product executive at a financial technology start-up, asked Muse to order windscreen wipers from the car-parts chain AutoZone. Seventeen hours later, the agent reported that the order had been cancelled because of an error and suggested that she buy the wipers on Amazon herself. As one technology executive put it after testing several agents, "It just doesn't feel magical yet."

Shops are hesitant too. When the software firm Human Forward tested agents on 200 websites, it found that about half of big retailers and popular brands do not let AI assistants shop on their sites. Amazon blocked Muse in September and has asked Meta to remove Amazon from the service. One likely reason is control. A retailer that lets an outside agent do the browsing loses the chance to show customers its own recommendations and advertisements, and Amazon's advertising business alone is expected to bring in $81.9 billion this year. Amazon's chief executive, Andy Jassy, nevertheless told investors in October that outside agents were not meaningfully affecting that business.

Beneath these commercial worries lies a legal question that nobody has fully answered. "If the bot gets it wrong, who's liable?" asks Mark Howell, of the e-commerce firm Rithum. Companies are giving very different answers. The electronics chain Best Buy treats an agent's purchases as if the customer had made them, and its terms state that it is not responsible for errors by any "Digital Agent." American Express, by contrast, has said it will protect eligible customers from charges caused by an agent's mistakes, while the bank JPMorgan Chase blocked outside agents from acting for its customers last month, citing security.

Optimists argue that this hesitation is temporary. In the 1990s, many people were nervous about typing their card details into a website, yet online shopping is now ordinary. As agents become more accurate and as rules on responsibility become clearer, they say, trust will follow. Sceptics reply that the problem is not only accuracy but independence. An agent that recommends products may be influenced by sponsored results, and a YouGov survey found that almost half of shoppers who use AI worry about exactly that. Handing over the final click also means handing over a moment of judgement that many people are not ready to give up.

For now, then, AI has become a powerful research tool rather than a trusted buyer. The numbers from this holiday season suggest that the technology is advancing faster than the agreements needed to support it. The real test for agentic commerce may not be whether a machine can press "buy", but whether anyone is clearly accountable when it presses the wrong button.

speak.p: Some people would happily let an AI agent do their routine shopping, such as buying groceries. Others prefer to make every purchase themselves. Which do you prefer, and why? Use specific reasons and examples.
speak.hint: State your choice; give two reasons (time saved, mistakes, control, privacy); add a personal example; finish with a one-sentence conclusion.

write.p:
Dr. Chen: AI shopping agents can now search for products and even pay for them, yet only a tiny share of purchases are made this way. Some people think we should welcome agents because they save time and money. Others think handing over payments to software is too risky. Should consumers let AI agents make purchases for them? Why or why not?
Lily: “I think agents are useful for boring, low-cost items like groceries. If a mistake costs only a few dollars, the time I save is worth it, and the technology will only get better.”
Marcus: “I disagree. Tests show agents still fail often, and nobody agrees on who pays when they get it wrong. Until the rules are clear, I want to press ‘buy’ myself.”
steps: Decide your position: welcome agents, reject them, or accept them only for some purchases.
Use one fact from the passage (e.g., 23 percent trust, 42.8 percent failure rate).
Respond to Lily or Marcus by name and add a new idea, such as sponsored results or privacy.
End with a clear one-sentence conclusion.

articles.title: Nvidia Hits Pause: Can Export Controls Keep Up with the Cloud?
articles.dek: Nvidia has stopped sending AI servers to four Southeast Asian countries. Can rules built for ships and customs officers control computing power that travels through cables?
paras: Nvidia, the company whose chips power much of the world's artificial intelligence, has halted shipments of servers containing its AI chips to four Southeast Asian countries: Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. According to reports in the Financial Times and The Wall Street Journal, its manufacturing partners Dell and Super Micro have told customers that Nvidia will not authorise their orders. The pause will last for an unspecified period while Nvidia checks whether its regional partners are meeting American export requirements, and it remains unclear whether the suspension is temporary.

The decision is the latest chapter in a long contest over advanced computing. Since 2022, the United States has restricted the sale of its most powerful AI chips to China, arguing that the technology could strengthen China's military and its ability to compete in strategic industries. Those rules were designed for a world of physical goods: they controlled where boxes of chips and servers could be sent. Increasingly, however, the most valuable resource in AI is not the chip itself but access to the computing power it provides.

That shift opened a loophole. A company does not need to own a server in order to use it; it can rent processing time from a data centre on the other side of a border and send its work there over the internet. Chinese AI developers have done exactly this, and the four Southeast Asian countries have become favoured destinations for their projects. The Institute for Progress, an American think tank, estimates that remote data centres of this kind supply about 24 percent of China's AI computing power, a share large enough to weaken the purpose of the original controls.

Earlier this month, the US Commerce Department moved to close that gap with new rules aimed at stopping Chinese companies from bypassing restrictions by renting computing power from cloud providers that use Nvidia chips. Under the new system, providers in the region need licences, and the industry has only a limited time to adjust. Businesses on the ground describe the rollout as confusing. "There's this new rule but no guidance on execution," one cloud executive told the Financial Times. Another warned that the uncertainty was "causing sheer chaos in the region."

The stakes are high for Nvidia as well. The company recorded $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, a 72 percent increase on the previous year, although part of that figure reflects sales booked in Singapore for customers elsewhere, including Taiwan and China. Southeast Asia has also become a fast-growing hub for new data centres, attracted by cheaper land, reliable power and a location between major markets. A prolonged pause could therefore slow investment that local governments have worked hard to attract.

Supporters of the crackdown argue that a control which can be avoided simply by logging in from another country is hardly a control at all. If Washington believes that cutting-edge AI should not flow to a strategic rival, they say, it must regulate access to computing power as well as the movement of hardware. In their view, Nvidia's pause is a sign that the rules are finally being taken seriously, and several Chinese AI developers have reportedly warned that losing overseas computing capacity could significantly slow their work.

Critics see a more complicated picture. They point out that Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia are not the targets of the policy, yet their businesses now face delays and higher costs. Some also argue that tighter limits may encourage China to accelerate the development of its own chips, reducing American influence in the long run. Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, has previously argued that allowing the company to sell its chips in China would help keep the country dependent on American technology. Others question whether any set of rules can keep pace when computing power can be moved across borders in seconds.

The pause therefore raises a question that goes far beyond one company. Export controls were invented for a world in which valuable goods crossed borders on ships and planes, where customs officers could inspect them. In the age of cloud computing, power travels through cables and can be rented by the hour from almost anywhere. Whether governments can draw borders in that invisible landscape, and how much collateral damage they are willing to accept while trying, may shape the global AI race for years to come.

articles.title: Dams on Thin Ice: Nepal's Hydropower Dilemma
articles.dek: Nepal needs winter electricity, but its glaciers are melting and its mountains shake. Should it build giant dams, or find a safer path to power?

sources.name: Schwanghart et al., Environmental Research Letters, 2016

paras: On 26 August, what appears to have been an avalanche on Langtang Lirung in central Nepal sent a churning wall of water, mud and boulders down the Bhotekoshi valley. The flood claimed many lives, and it also damaged at least a dozen hydropower projects. Three months later, as winter approaches and electricity runs short, the disaster has reopened one of Nepal's most difficult debates: should the country build large storage dams in the high Himalaya, or is the climate changing too quickly to make them safe?

Nepal depends heavily on hydropower, using the steep rivers that flow from Himalayan snow and glaciers. Almost all of its plants, however, are run-of-river schemes. Instead of holding water behind a tall wall, they divert part of a river's flow through turbines and return it downstream. This design is cheaper and less disruptive, but it has a serious weakness: when rivers shrink in the dry season, output drops to less than half of installed capacity. The country has only one storage plant, the four-decade-old Kulekhani, which generates 92 gigawatt-hours a year and helps meet winter peak demand.

The result is a seasonal mismatch. The Nepal Electricity Authority expects domestic plants to generate 1,218 megawatts this winter, against peak demand of 2,250 to 2,300 megawatts, and it reportedly plans to import 1,154 megawatts from India. Private generators, which supply nearly 60 percent of the country's electricity, have been reluctant to build reservoirs because of the steep costs and risks involved. For a country rich in rivers, relying on a neighbour for so much winter power is, to many Nepalis, both costly and frustrating.

Supporters of storage dams argue that reservoirs are the obvious solution. By capturing monsoon water and releasing it in winter, they could close the seasonal gap, cut imports and protect water supplies for cities and farms. Two major projects are under way: the Tanahu Seti dam, with storage of 300 million cubic metres, is scheduled to begin operating next year, while the 263-metre Budhigandaki dam is expected to cost around $2.77 billion. "High dams are safe if geological studies are properly conducted and designed with the latest technology," says the geologist Bishal Nath Upreti.

Opponents point to how rapidly the mountains themselves are changing. An assessment by ICIMOD, a regional research centre, suggests that under current emissions pathways about 80 percent of the Himalaya's present glacier volume will be gone by 2100. As glaciers melt, the lakes that form behind them grow larger and more unstable, raising the risk of a glacial lake outburst flood. A 2016 study found that two-thirds of 257 sampled Himalayan hydropower plants sit on potential routes of such floods. The danger is not theoretical: in 2023, a flood from a glacial lake destroyed the Teesta III dam in the neighbouring Indian state of Sikkim. One former government secretary, Dwarika Nath Dhungel, says that people in the valleys are "living just below an atom bomb of the glacial lakes."

Earthquakes add a second layer of uncertainty. Nepal sits where the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates collide, and the 2015 earthquake temporarily cost the country more than 30 percent of its hydropower production. A former head of the electricity authority, Hitendra Dev Shakya, supports reservoirs but admits the limits of engineering: "The dam is strong enough to withstand a magnitude 7 quake, but what about 8 or above?" Engineers also warn that if every dam had to be designed to survive a flood like the one in August, many projects might no longer be financially feasible.

Some experts believe Nepal should look in a different direction altogether. Himanshu Thakkar of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People favours solar power combined with pumped storage, in which water is pumped uphill when electricity is plentiful and released through turbines when it is needed. Because such systems can be built away from major rivers, they avoid many flood risks. Researchers have counted about 2,800 suitable sites in Nepal, and one model put the cost of solar plus storage at about 8.5 US cents per kilowatt-hour, compared with the 6.7 cents the electricity authority pays in the dry season. Both studies, however, are models rather than tested projects.

Between these positions, some officials are searching for a middle path. Bibek Raj Kandel, an adviser to the energy minister, argues that Nepal should look "beyond a binary pro- and anti-dam stance" and choose projects that match each valley's climate, terrain and grid needs. He also warns that "the real danger zone is the construction period," when a half-built dam is especially vulnerable. Nepal's choice will matter well beyond its borders, because every mountain country facing melting glaciers must decide how much risk it is prepared to accept in return for reliable power.

parts.title: Multiple-choice cloze
parts.task: Read the text and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.
parts.text: Artificial intelligence {1} centre stage in this year's holiday shopping, yet few people are ready to let it {2} the bill. Most shoppers are happy to use chatbots to {3} inspiration for gifts, but they draw the {4} at handing over their card details. Their caution has been {5} out by recent tests, in which agents often bought the wrong items. Many retailers have also {6} a firm stance against outside agents, fearing that they will lose control of their customers. Until it is clear who is to {7} when things go wrong, the technology is unlikely to {8} on with the general public.

parts.text: For decades, export controls worked {9} a simple principle: if a product could not cross a border, it could not be used on the other side. Critics argue that the new rules arrived with little warning, leaving businesses unsure {13} to comply. {14} the confusion, supporters insist that a rule which can be avoided so easily is {15} better than no rule at all. items.why: Something works “on” (or “upon”) a principle.
“Turn something on its head” means to change it completely.
A defining relative clause about things needs “which” or “that” as the subject.
“That is why” refers back to the previous sentence to introduce a result.
“Unsure how to comply” means not knowing the way to do it.

“No/little better than” means almost the same as, here showing the rule is almost worthless.
The verb “depend” is followed by “on” or “upon”.

“But” signals a contrast, so a negative adjective is needed: “unstable”.
“With little” is followed by a noun: “with little warning”.
After “their” we need a noun; “confide” → “confidence”.

parts.title: Key word transformation
parts.task: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Use between three and six words, including the word given.

items.s1: Shoppers are reluctant to let AI agents pay for their purchases.
